title: A fake ISI mark: possession is not use

scenes.dialogue: Hi, I am Ravishankar from LawWorld. A factory holds a roller bearing a fake I S I mark. Is possessing it an offence, without proof that the mark was used?
scenes.shown: Hi, I am Ravishankar from LawWorld. A factory holds a roller bearing a fake ISI mark. Is possessing it an offence, without proof that the mark was used?

scenes.dialogue: On fourteenth October, twenty twenty six, the Kerala High Court, through a single bench of Honourable Justice A Badharudeen, answered that question.
scenes.shown: On 14 October 2026, the Kerala High Court, through a single bench of Honourable Justice A. Badharudeen, answered that question.

scenes.dialogue: The Bureau of Indian Standards alleged that its officials, inspecting a firm's factory, found a roller with a spurious I S I mark, and no valid licence.
scenes.shown: The Bureau of Indian Standards alleged that its officials, inspecting a firm's factory, found a roller with a spurious ISI mark, and no valid licence.

scenes.dialogue: It said a spurious mark was also on the factory wall, and filed a complaint against the firm and its four partners under the B I S Act, nineteen eighty six.
scenes.shown: It said a spurious mark was also on the factory wall, and filed a complaint against the firm and its four partners under the BIS Act, 1986.

scenes.dialogue: The Taliparamba Magistrate found no cogent proof that the firm used the mark on any article. No finished product bearing the fake mark was produced.
Nor was the roller's seizure properly proved, to show it worked and could apply the mark. In January twenty ten, all the accused were acquitted.
scenes.shown: Nor was the roller's seizure properly proved, to show it worked and could apply the mark. In January 2010, all the accused were acquitted.

scenes.dialogue: On appeal, the Bureau argued mere possession of a fake I S I mark was enough, without proof of use. The firm and its partners said possession alone is no offence.
scenes.shown: On appeal, the Bureau argued mere possession of a fake ISI mark was enough, without proof of use. The firm and its partners said possession alone is no offence.

scenes.dialogue: The High Court held: Sections Eleven and Twelve prohibit the use of the mark. The legislature chose the word use, and never meant mere possession to be punished there.
scenes.shown: The High Court held: Sections 11 and 12 prohibit the use of the mark. The legislature chose the word "use", and never meant mere possession to be punished there.

scenes.dialogue: Possessing an object that can affix such a mark, without evidence of its use in making goods, does not attract those sections. The Bureau's appeal was dismissed.
